blocks.x: Let me make a note of the date. This is May the 28th, 1961 and we're over at 731 St. Peter Street interviewing Harry Shields and Johnny Riggs is good enough to arrange the interview and his present here too and this is Bill Russell. Johnny you have something that you want to make

a remark first. Since Harry played with Emmett Hardy so much I'd like to know, there's been a lot of discussion about what style Emmett played in, I'd like to ask Harry what he remembers about his style. He played with Emmett Hardy in Brownlee's band before I joined it and he played with Emmett Hardy I guess maybe more than anybody else in New Orleans. I think he told me
he played in Emmett's first band, right Harry? I think so John, that was the first band he organized up at, we opened the Midway Park up at, what was it, Harvey's Canal there, across the river?
On the other side of the river? On the other side of the river. Midway Park.

Midway Park. Yeah, I don't remember. And I remember he played very good. You don't uh... Might I say he played an original style. Ah. Very good. Did he live over across the river at that time? He did, he lived over in Algea's at that time and he played real fine. Fine cornet. Must have been very young. We might ask him...
He was, he was young. If you don't mind to give your birth date and your full name too,
if you have a middle name or anything. My, my birth date, goes way back.

1899. That's not so bad. My name is Harry Shields. Yeah, have any middle name or initial or any... P. Harry P. Shields. Um, we might get a little bit of background on your life first to tell about your family. Did your father play any instrument or mother?

No, my father was a dancer. He was a dancer. Yeah, he did clog and buck and wings, soft shoe. Did he travel in any shows? So did my grandmother. No, no, they weren't professionals. Just for their own amusement. And his whole family, they were all dancers. Yeah. But my mother's family were all musicians. Did your mother play some instrument? No, my mother didn't, but her brothers did. And so did her mother. Her mother played guitar. Yeah. And she had, let's see there, one, two, three... I... Yeah, three brothers. They all played string instruments, violin, mandolin, guitar, bass.
Uh, how many brothers did you have? Any other brothers beside, uh, Larry?

Yeah, I had two half brothers, John and James. Did they ever play music? Yeah, yeah. James played, uh, uh, all string instruments and he played a cornet too. Were their name, uh, Shields? Do you... No, Ruth. R-U-T-H. Ruth. Ruth. And my mother married twice. Yeah.

Yeah. Um, are they still living by any chance? No, no. They died. And how much older was, uh, Larry than, uh, you? Six years. Six years. I think we have, uh, several accounts of his life. You know, the jazz club had the whole issue.

I had a brother between Larry and I, played piano. Edward. Edward. I think you played with him, didn't you, John? Did you know him? Ed, the piano player? He played with Sharky and, uh, he played with Emmett too. Oh. And, uh, we had a little band with Emmett. I think I heard him. Ed played piano. Sure. And we had Charlie Leach on drums then. And, uh, oh, uh, let's see, Donald Coleman on violin. You remember Don.
Donald Coleman, he was the president of the Times-Picay Union, right? Right, right. That's right. And, uh... What did he play? Violin. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah.

And, uh, we used to have little... We used to go out to Charlie Leach's house when he lived out on Harmony, near Britannia. Ah. And, uh, Teddy Hart was always out there too, and, uh, Frank Mackey. Red Mackey? Red, yeah, Red Mackey. And we'd always...
Red was in everything in music, wasn't he?

We'd get together and, no, we'd have a lot of fun, Emmett and Charlie. Oh, Emmett too, huh? Uh-huh. And we'd get out there and play and have a lot of fun. We were all kids. Ed on the piano. Sometimes Frank would play piano with us. And, uh, we went on a convention. I don't remember what year it was, but we were kids with the Chalamual Grotto, Kansas City, Missouri. Oh, yeah. And we had Leon Smallow on trombone. Mm. And Ed on piano. Donald on the violin. Charlie Leach on drums. And myself on clarinet. We had a picture made.
No, no clarinet of trumpet, huh?
Well, Emmett played clarinet. Oh, Emmett.
Damn it. He was with you? Oh, yeah.

Kansas City. Yeah, Kansas City on a convention. And we had a picture made then. Monk Hazel says he had one. The, uh, the photographer from the Star Newspaper Office, they give us a nice write-up. The paper took a picture of the band on a truck, you know. Uh-huh. And, uh, incidentally, Max Blanchard happened to be on the truck. He was one of the prophets, you know. You know, Max Blanchard. Yeah, I know. Max Blanchard. And a few other guys. How old were you? Can you figure out about what year that was? I think I must have been about 16 or 17. So it would be around 1916. I think I was a couple of years older than Emmett. Well, Emmett was just a kid then.
Yeah.

And that was before we opened the Midway Park. But, uh, we did play a few jobs then, yes. We played the Young Women's Christian Association on Saturday night. A few other little jobs. My brother had one piano then, but when we went up to the Midway, Emmett organized the other band. We didn't have a piano.
How long has your brother Ed been dead now?
Ed died in 1938.
38. I never even knew about it. Uh, I wonder if you could tell us a little bit how you happened to take up clarinet. Was that your first instrument? Yeah.
Well, my brother Larry started me off when I was a little kid.
Did you use his horn at first? Yeah. I used Larry's horn.
He'd teach me little tunes, you know. Well, he was a kid himself.
What kind of a clarinet did he have? No doubt an Albert, I guess. Albert system, yeah.
Uh-huh. At that time he had, uh, I remember well, it was a buffet.
Buffet. About how many keys do you remember? Thirteen keys. Thirteen, yeah. I've seen some of those.

Then, uh, after he, uh, went up north, he was in Chicago. Of course, I knew quite a bit about the clarinet then, but I didn't own one. How old were you when you started, about? About that time, when he first started me off, I was just a little fellow about eight years old, And he'd teach me a few little simple tunes on the clarinet. But then when he left home, I didn't have a clarinet and didn't play at all. So, uh, when he got to Chicago, man, of course I was a few years older then, I decided I wanted to practice the clarinet. Yeah. So I wrote him, he sent me the old thirteen key clarinet. He bought himself a new one. And my brother Jimmy, who was a very good musician, the one I told you that played all the strings and the cornet, well, he had never tried to play a clarinet, but he did finger it and he figured it out. So he helped me along with the clarinet. And...
Did you learn to read at that time ever?
No, not at that time, but later on I got a... Self-instruct, you know, taught myself a few little things I could get by. Well...
What was your very first job or even first band that you played with?

Alfred Lane. Alfred Lane. Alfred Lane. Called him Pansy Lane. I played with him before I played with Emmett. And then I worked with him a while playing prize fights around the street, you know, advertising rather. And we went to work at the old Pup Cafe on Ivorville Street and worked there a while. Then I worked across the street at the Raleigh Rye with my brother Ed on the piano and a boy by the name of Willie Rich on drums. Yeah. And I left there. And Leon... Charlie Cadillo took my place. All right. And then I quit playing for a while. My father was a contractor, a painter contractor. And I went to work with my father.
Well, what part of town were you raised in and where were you... What part of town were you born in and all?
Uh, well I was born on First Street, First and Liberty. 2319 First Street.
When we were... When I was about five or six years old, we moved to Third, Third and Clara. And we lived there up until about 1928. And we moved right back in Broadmoor, where I'm living now. Yes.

Of course... When I talked to you about, oh, it's been, I guess, 10 years ago, once at the famous door, I think you told me you remembered when you were a boy hearing music up in the neighborhood, some of the colored... Was it Buddy Bolin or somebody near there?
Well, there were a lot of colored people around there. Well, Buddy Bolin, I really didn't know him. He, I think he died before my time, but my older brothers knew him.
Yep. I think he...

Jimmy, he just died about a little over a year ago. He was, I think, 71, 72, maybe a little over a year. When he died. He was in his seventies, yeah. Well, he knew Buddy Bolin. Uh-huh. And Buddy lived two doors from us, so he told me.
Uh-huh.

And, uh, I have an older sister. She's still living. She's the only relative I have now. She's a half-sister. Yeah. She's in her eighties. And she knew Buddy Bolin and his sister and mother when she was young. Well, they're spoken about Buddy. My brother, especially, he's spoken about him quite a bit.
Jim?
Jim, yeah. He said he was a real fine cornet player and he took sick, mentally ill, and he was confined. And then he came out and when he came out, my brother said he played fine trombone.
Played trombone then later?
Played fine trombone. He said he practiced the trombone while he was confined.
Uh-huh.
And he came out and played trombone. He said he played very good. Uh-huh. But, uh, then he went back and I understand he died there.
Yes, I think he died in 1931. Uh-huh. I think he was committed to the asylum in 1907, I believe is the date.
Uh-huh.
So you would have only been seven or eight years old when that happened. Yeah.
Yeah.
I don't remember for sure. That's one advantage in having the tape recording. We can remember what people say from now on. Uh-huh. When I first talked to you, I think he said that.
Jimmy never mentioned when he was committed.
Yeah, I think you told me once you'd maybe heard Johnny Dodds, was it? Or?

Oh, I used to listen to Johnny Dodds a lot. Did he live near you? I don't know where he lived, but he used to play at Naulties Hall and Josephine between Magnolia and South Robinson. That wasn't too far from where I lived. Oh, definitely. And of course, I studied in the clarinet, you know, and I was interested and naturally I'd just go down there and sit across the street on the step all night long and listen to him. Listen. Or wherever there was a band.
Yeah.
I'd get there and listen, you know. And especially if it was a clarinet play, I liked Mike. And I liked Johnny Dodds.
How old were you then? Of course, I never heard him in the old days. I heard him right before he died in Chicago and in some of his records. And I don't know how he played pretty well.
I thought he played very good. He worked with Joe Oliver. Joe Oliver. Uh-huh. I think they played there two or three nights a week at Naulties Hall.
But how old would you have been then? You'd already taken up the clarinet then.
Oh, I'd say that was during World War I.
How about that?
Maybe a little before. Yeah. Maybe a little after. I don't remember, but I was quite young.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh.

Uh-huh. And of course, I'd go back to National Baseball Park, which was just two blocks from where I lived. They'd have dances there on Monday night. They'd usually have three or four colored bands there.
Was that open to whites or was that a colored band?
No, it was a colored band.
Oh, because you could hear it outside. Yeah.
I'd sit out on the banks of the Claiborne Canal. It was an open canal.
Oh, yeah. I remember that too.
Lots of times, Emmett would come to the house and he and I both would go out and listen to the bands, you know.
Yeah. Do you know any of the bands you heard there? The name anymore?
Yeah. Sam Morgan played there and Rene, Kid Rene and Punch.
Oh, yeah. Remember Punch that he played there?

And all the different bands about that time who were, you know, playing around all the colored bands, they played out there. They'd lay these platforms, sections, you know, on the ground. Yeah. It was a regular ballpark.
And dance on that then.
Dance on that, yeah. Mm-hmm. Took in a square ground then.
Yeah.
And now that's a school.
Right on Claiborne then.
Claiborne and Third.
Third, yeah.
Well, from Claiborne to Willow, Third to Second, took in that whole square.
Do you remember much about your brother playing down here? Did you get to hear him very much with other bands other than Nick LaRocca and that group?
Well, he played with different bands, yeah. He played with Jack Lane and Larry.
That's Larry, huh?
Larry, yeah. That's where he left.

We saw Jack Lane on Friday. They took a television movie for the educational television station. He's going to have a little interview and movie with him some of these days on there. Yeah. He's in good health, looked pretty good. He does. His wife is all right too, but she has trouble with her legs now. Oh, she does. He can't walk very well. Did you ever get to play with Papa Lane yourself?

I think I played only one job with him. Well, I was really playing with his son. With his son. His son played cornet, but he happened to play bass drum. I think we played a parade one day. Georgie Brunas was playing some wrong, and I think Emmet Rogers played the snare drum that day, and Jack played bass drum. Of course, we were kids then.
Yeah. He said he had a lot of boys working for him. All the Brunas brothers were pretty young when they worked for him and started with him.
Yeah, yeah.
He always had a bunch of young kids. He said some of them stayed at his house even.

Well, I imagine Jack just about gave all these guys their first start in the music business. And of course I've had quite a few to tell me that, such as Nick LaRocka, Larry. But Larry played with quite a few bands around here before he left, he played with the marching bands, you know, and played with Joe Ella Bush. I remember he had his conductor's cap and he just changed the name of the band, you know, and just put it over the cap and drive it. And I have a picture taken in 1907 when Larry played with the St. Francis de Sales Band. I have that picture at home. He and Clem Camp. Do you remember Clem? Did you ever hear of him? I think he's still living.
What did he play?
Clarinet. Yeah?
Yeah.
He's one of the old timers. I imagine now he's... Clem Camp. Clem Camp. I imagine he's in his 70s now. He lives somewhere on Talladonna near Galvis. I think he's still alive.
I'll try to find him.
Yeah. Yeah. And he's one of the old timers.
Must be.
And he and Larry played in that St. Francis de Sales Band together. And I don't know if Clem ever went away and left New Orleans.

Well, speaking of other clarinetists, on this old Edison machine, this is one of the old time machines, it has these real thick... We found a few records with the Yellow Nunez and the Louisiana Five. Do you remember anything about Yellow Nunez hearing him much?
Well, Yellow was a very fine clarinet player. I heard him quite a few times, yeah.
On these records they don't have a carnet, just... No, I understand he...
At that time he played a C clarinet.
Oh, I didn't know it was a C clarinet.
Mm-hmm.
And he took the lead, of course, then on these records. Mm-hmm.
He played a C Albert system clarinet at that time and used trombone.

He must have played a C that time he came down here and played with Brownlee a little while. You remember when he played with Brownlee a little while when I was with him? Because it was a little short clarinet. It was. It was probably the C clarinet.
I didn't pay any attention. He liked to play the C clarinet, I know. I don't remember that, John, when he played with Brownlee.
Not long, but just a few jobs.
By the way, did you ever play any other thing except B flat?
Well, I played saxophone.
You never had the E flat, the little short one in the band or anything?
No, no, I've never had occasion.
Did Larry, do you know, play anything?
I don't think so. I think Larry always used the B flat.
Did he play sax too? I don't remember.

Larry played sax, yeah. He worked with a few big bands after he left the Dixieland Band. Yes. Worked out in California. He worked with Harold MacDonald and a couple of the big bands. Played saxophone and the clarinet. I have pictures at home. These big bands he worked with. And he worked in a show out there. With, I think, a 14-piece band.
Do you know about what age Larry got started?
On the clarinet?
On the clarinet when you were a boy?
Well, Larry, Larry was, I'd imagine Larry was young, about 15, 16.
Do you remember him practicing at home before he could play well? I don't think that's when he was just learning or anything?

Yes, I do remember that. He bought his first clarinet from a fellow by the name of Freddie Burns, who played with my brother Jimmy and played with King Watsky and Buzz Harvey, played bass. And they used to have a little band. They'd go out and play house parties. They all had day jobs, work days, and go out at night, you know, mostly on Saturday and Sunday, play all day picnics and all. And Freddie Burns sold Larry his first clarinet and gave Larry a few pointers on the clarinet. Well, Larry never did reading either, you know, not much anyhow.
He learned himself then, mostly from then on.
Yeah, had a self-instructor. And so he, he'd play with the King Watsky too, you know, and my brother Jimmy.
Did Larry ever say who his favorite clarinetists were when he was coming up? If anybody older than he was that he listened to?
No, he never mentioned anyone, not to me, anyhow.
What type of music did your mother's folks play? Would it be with a good beat to it, like jazz, or was it a different style? What would you say?

Well, my mother, my mother died in 1948, and she was the youngest of four children, so I understand. And she was 94 when she died in 48, so therefore her brothers were much older than her. She said there's quite a few years between her and her youngest brother, her brother Tony, who played guitar. And she first married, she was 18. And she said her brothers got together and they played for her wedding. And she said they didn't read music at all.
They were fakers then too.

They were fakers then, but they didn't use a clarinet. She said a fellow by the name of, she didn't say, yeah, she said P-Nots, not P-Nots, P-Nots. He played the flute with this string band. They had a bass and a violin, a mandolin, two guitars, and a flute.
Do you suppose it was anything like jazz?

And she said even though they played, well she said ragtime, or jazz, she said yeah they could play mazurkas and shottish. And she even said that the fellow played the flute, worked for the sanitation department, and drove a dump cart, you know. Yeah.
Yeah.
But she said he was a very fine musician.
He was a regular flute. Flute player. A regular flute player.
Uh huh. So therefore they were evidently playing jazz then, what we call jazz now. And she said they, none of her brothers could read music. Yeah. Neither could her mother.

You know, Nick LaRocca makes a big point that it all started with the original Dixieland and there was not anything you could call jazz before that. Of course they probably were the first ones to use that name.

They were the first ones to use that name. Larry told me that. He said that's true. Now Larry was very truthful. I never knew of Larry to ever tell a lie. He told me that. He said they were working at the Casino Gardens in Chicago. And the band was going pretty good. And they were getting a real good salary of $35 a week then. You see. So that was in 1915 or 16. And some fella come in and said, Jazz are up. You know, he said he was half loaded. So they said, huh? What was that? He said, Jazz. That's Jazz are up, man. You know. Larry says, and Nick said, sounds good. Never heard the word before. That's what we have here. We have jazz. We've got a jazz band. So they put a big sign out the next day. The original Dixieland Jazz Band. J-A-S. Yeah.
The first records they have had that. J-A-S.
And then later it was J-A-S-S. Then later, J-A-Z. Then J-A-Z-Z. Now that's what I was told. Now, where the word originated. I don't know. I wasn't there.
I was just wondering about the style of the music itself. Do you think they were playing a similar style, like Jack Lane's band, maybe way back? Before the Dixieland group or not?
I thought it was a little more, well might I say, more modern then.
The Dixieland Band The Dixieland Band Okay, let's go.

Yeah, Larry, he liked the Fournier Reed, and he always told me that he had trouble with reeds when he was with the Dixieland Band at Rising Weathers. And he'd go around buying different brands of reeds, trying reeds. So he happened to go into this little store, over on the east side somewhere, and this guy was a violin maker. But he had these reeds, and Larry said when he bought a few of the reeds, and he tried them out. He said the reeds were so wonderful that he went back and bought a couple of gross. He bought all the reeds that the guy had. Did the man make them himself? No, it was a French reed.
Oh, imported.
Yeah. And so he asked the man if he could order him some more. So the guy kept him supplied with reeds, and he never used anything after that. Fournier Reed.
No matter what part of the country he was in, he'd send for them, huh?

He'd send for them, yeah. Well, he always kept a good supply of them. He said he'd never had any trouble. He'd just put the reed on there, and it would blow wonderfully. And like I say, he used this buffet wooden mop piece, and he used the buffet. And he got his new clarinet.
Was it buffet too? Yeah. He liked that. He liked that. It had more keys or rings on in the early one?
No, it was only a 17 key clarinet. 17.
That's more than a 13 key.
Yeah, I have it.
What kind of instrument do you have now?
Well, I use a pencil mullet.
Pencil mullet. You still use the albert, of course.
Albert, yeah. Full albert.
Is that an improved albert? This is a Selmer. Oh, Selmer.
What do you, why do you prefer an albert over a BAME system?
I guess it's on account of the boar, Johnny. On account of what? The boar. I imagine.
Oh, the boar.
No, I may be wrong about that, but it just seems as though I get a fatter tone at the albert. Well, everybody says the same name. Maybe it's just my imagination. No, I don't think so either.
I've questioned a lot of clarinetists. Even some symphony men that play the BAME system will admit that the others got a bigger tone and more metal or something.
Well, I spoke to a clarinet player in New York. He was from England. And he told me that most clarinet players over in Europe use the albert system. They still do.
But I didn't know that.

That's what he said now. I've never been to Europe. And that's what he told me. And he told me he played the albert clarinet. And he said he liked the albert because you've got a broader tone. I said, well, I thought it was my imagination. Because I have heard BAME clarinet players who've got a pretty broad tone too. You know, like Kenny Devine gets a nice fat tone out of the BAME. So does Benny Goodman. Yeah, I've heard fat tones. Benny Goodman gets a fat tone out of the BAME.
Yeah, but still I've heard Benny Goodman when you don't have a microphone sometime and it doesn't come through like when he's up close to the mic. Is that right?
It sounds big too. Uh-huh. Tony Perrini gets a big fat tone. He gets a fat tone, yeah.
Oh, bang. Tony, he plays a BAME.
Yeah, there are some people.
Yeah. Peter Fountain gets a big fat tone too. He gets a big fat tone.
He does too. There's something about the albert. I wonder sometimes if it's imagination too, but still the symphony players even say that. I've got a BAME at home.

Now I took the same out piece off the albert and put it on the BAME. Maybe it was me, you know. Maybe not the clarinet. Maybe it was, I was just impressed that I wouldn't get the big tone and I didn't. You know, I got the thin tone off the BAME. Maybe it was a clarinet. It's not such a good one. Cheap clarinet.
What kind of a reed do you like to use? About how hard and what makes...
Oh, I use two, two and a half.
Rather soft and it's hardly...
Yeah.
On the soft side at least.
Yeah. I prefer the number two string.

Yeah. Do you like more of the keys and then what about that old 13 key instrument? Did it seem easier when you got more keys on it and the rings and all that were better in tune? Or why did you change? Of course they don't make, I guess, the 13 key hardly anymore.
I don't imagine so. Well, albert clarinets are hard to find.
Yeah. They don't hardly make any alberts.

Well, these two clarinets I got now were given to me in New York. Kenny Devine gave them to me. They're both very good clarinets. Full albert system. And he played the BAME. He started on the BAME, studied the BAME, then switched to the alberts. Played the alberts for quite a few years. Now he's back playing the BAME. And he gave me a couple of his alberts clarinets.
What do you mean by the full albert? Some people use the term improved albert. Does it have three little keys here on the left hand?
Yeah, this is unimproved albert. The improved has three little keys. The pencil is much more improved than this.

Remember there's one pencil muller I picked up about two months ago, even in the joint where you put the two joints together. There's a little hole coming through there. That's the kind of keys. Yeah, but I know what you mean. Yeah, they have almost as many keys.
It's called the full albert system.
A lot of trill keys there.
Yeah. Bill Bourgeois plays the same system. Yeah, that's right.
I know he.
Bill Bourgeois plays the same way. Mm-hmm.

Is there anything, when you first learned, that you could tell us about anything that helped you to learn to master the clarinet, to get a tone, any secrets that is in learning to get that broad tone or that your brother helped you with? I'm not trying to pry into your secrets or anything, but I mean if there is anything, it would be a benefit to other players someday. It's good not to have that knowledge lost.
Well, I don't know.
Any advice that he gave you on how to blow or what to do?
Well, he did tell me to relax and don't use too much pressure.
With your lips so that you have to bite it too hard.
Yeah. So I don't use too much pressure.
He only used a medium. He didn't use a hard read then.
No, I don't think Larry ever used a real hard read.
Can you tell us some more about some of the jobs you played? You mentioned a couple of these early jobs with the...
Oh, well, I played with Johnny, Johnny Hyman, I guess, haven't I? Years back with Brown Lee.
Yeah, with Brown Lee.
I worked with Sharky Bonanno when we were young.
Let's see, was Tom Brown in the... Tom, yeah. In that Brown Lee band?
I played quite a bit with Tom, yeah. With Brown Lee and of course with Johnny, Johnny Ways. And we made some nice recordings.
And by the way, when were the first records that you ever made? Can you remember? That was with Brown Lee's band.
I think it was 1924 and 25. Yeah, we have...
An all okay record. Yeah, we have that record up at Tulane now. I wish I had it here to play for you and get your reaction. I don't have a copy here.
Those were your compositions, weren't there, Harry? One of them was.
Yeah, those are the shields on there. When I first found the record, I thought it was your brother. Of course, that was 20 years ago and I knew more about your brother then than you.

See, Brown Lee, he was... That was his introduction to Peculiar Rank. Norman Brown Lee? Yeah. And of course, the other side was Sharky's tune. Let's see, what was the name of that? Dirty Rank. Oh, yeah. Yeah. So we decided that we'd use three names on both sides. But the verse and the chorus of Peculiar was really mine. And then later Sharky recorded it again, I think with Sidney Airdman and Mel Kaisel. So he told me about this. Well, go ahead. You can make a recording. Go ahead.

By the way, Dick Allen, who works with us up at Tulane, was over in Pensacola just two weeks ago and interviewed Norman Brown. Norman, did he? Said he's getting along fine. He's president of the union over there. I understand that.
He's a great fellow.
And I think he's president of the Kiwanis Club or some other club. Oh, he is? In the community, too. He seems to be a prominent fellow in the community over there, too.
We played lots of jobs together. He's a great fellow.
Sorry I didn't get to meet him, but I've still never seen him. Remember anything about the dates you played? The most of where the jobs were? What's the special engagements?
Oh, my. We used to play, oh, seven nights a week at that time. I guess we got...
The midway was the standard, wasn't it? Yeah, the midway.

The steady. At the park, that was? Yeah, we used to play the Knights of Columbus, the Elks home, the Elks River Garden, and, oh, the Knights Pythian over in Algiers, and the public school dances. Well, we worked seven nights a week. And, gee, and at the end of the week, well, we'd all get out our books and Norman would give us the jobs for the following week, you know, and we'd just write them down what time they'd start and what time.
Yeah. Well, when you played at the Midway Park, for instance, what were they for? Just night dances and at night time and...
Yeah, yeah, regular dances.
Did they have a pavilion or where did they dance?
Yes, it was a regular pavilion. Yeah, big platform.
Ooh, great, vast...
Open air place, you know.
They had a bandstand built out, sticking out from that platform in the back. And the bandstand was enclosed. Yeah. In the back.
Yeah, but no roof over the dancers or... Oh, yeah. It was over there, too? Yeah. Yeah, it was a... A regular dance pavilion, that was up near the Harvey Canal, huh? Yeah.
Yeah, that was above Harvey. Took the Napoleon Avenue Ferry.
Oh, yeah.

No, the Louisiana Ferry, wasn't it? Between Louisiana and Napoleon. Was it? That's right, it was between the ferries. Was that... That wasn't Westwood, you know, was it? I know it was above Harvey. I think. I remember the old streetcar used to switch there and come back to Algiers. Do you remember that?
Yeah.
And then, last time we rode the streetcar. Yeah. And Algiers streetcar. What kind of a park was it?
For picnics in the daytime or anything like that? Or did it have...

Well, it wasn't a regular park. It was just a big sort of a... Just a regular dance pavilion. It was like a cow pasture. Yeah. With this thing, it was built. Well, then it didn't it. Now, sometimes, I imagine the churches would give fairs there on the ground, on the earth. Yeah. You know? And the dancing would be part of that, you know? Wasn't anything like that? They most likely hide the whole cow pasture, you see?
Yeah. Wouldn't it be like Pontchartrain, we have a ferris wheel? The fellow that ran off.

Oh, no, no, no. The only thing it had was this big dance. It was an open dance hall. The sides were open and it had a roof on it and had... It was about six feet off of the ground, huh? Five feet off of the ground. Oh, was it? Four feet off of the ground, something like that. I don't remember that.

I know when I opened up the place, the platform was on the ground and we had a canvas tarpaulin over the dance floor then, Emmett and Joe Lloyd Cannon, and Chink. Well, we sat outside the dance floor and had regular shavings, wood shavings out there, you know? And we sat there then. Yeah. The first night we opened the midway. But then they put a roof over there and had a real nice dance floor, a bandstand, you know? I think it was the guy's name that ran the place. His name was Everett Thomas C., wasn't he?
I was about to ask you. That name is familiar, Thomas C., I must have heard it somewhere. Everett Thomas C., yeah.
Thomas C., Thomas C., Everett Thomas C., yeah.
He was a nice fellow.
Yeah. Remember that? He really was, yeah.
He would be too old to be living now, I guess. You can't tell. Some of us...
Well, he was a good deal older than us and we're 61.

Well, I met a fellow not so long ago now, whether it was in New York or Cleveland, where, I don't remember now, but he happened to mention that he told some of the boys in the band that he was Everett Thomas C.'s relative somewhere. May have said son.
Yeah.

But, oh, I said Everett Thomas C., I said, well, I worked for him when I was a kid. The old midway, he said, well, that's why I mentioned that. I figured you must have played music there if you were from New Orleans. I said, yes, I did. In fact, I opened the place up. Now, I don't remember just what the relation he was to Everett Thomas C., but he was a relation.
By the way, in the old days, did you travel much, any of the bands you were with, did they get out of New Orleans?

Well, when I was a kid, I was playing around with Lane at the time. It was Pansy Lane. Yeah, Pansy Lane. And Jimmy Durante wanted me to join his band in New York. And Pansy Lane did join him, and Jack Loycanna on trombone. And Arnold, the deacon, on piano. No, on bass, that's right. He played bass with Jimmy Durante and Lane played the cornet. But he wanted me to join him. And then later on, Frank Christian was in New York. He wrote me. He wanted me to join him. But my mother said, well, I've got two boys away now. Well, Larry was with the Dixon Band Band, and Eddie, he was in Chicago working with Emil Christian, and I think, Yellen Nunes. And she said, no, I don't want you to go away. Staying home. She's staying home. So, then Ed went with the Dixon Band Band for a couple of weeks, right after Regis died. But I don't know what happened. He probably got home sick. He came on back home, and they got a fellow by the name of Sidney Mansfield, who I understand is a movie director now, California. And he left the band, and they got Frankie Signy rallying for a while, and they got Russell Rousey.
He stayed with him. He stayed with him.
Then when they went to England, Russell had to come back to New York for some reason rather than that. They got a piano player by the name of Billy Jones. And he stayed with him until they left.
Did they get him in New York?
No.
Over in London.
Oh, he was an English piano player.
Yeah, I understand. I think it was Larry told me before he died. He had a pub in London called Two Keys or Cross Keys or something like that. And he's still in London.
Yeah, I think people have written articles about him over in the English papers occasionally.
Well, he's one of the authorities on Dixon Land Jazz over there. Larry said he was a very good piano player.
Did Larry ever write much when he'd be on these tours, write letters back home? Oh, yes.
He wrote my mother off at least once a week, and he did write me a lot of letters.
When the records came out down here, did they cause much excitement? They sure did.
Yeah. Mm-hmm.

You know, according to one report, they wrote in an editorial once in one of the papers here as if they were sort of ashamed of the jazz having a New Orleans name, you know, like it was low-class music.
Yeah, I didn't read the article, but I remember my father talking about it.
Did the people in general feel that way, or were they proud of the band, or what do you think?
I thought the people in general were very proud of the band.
I should think they would have been. I just wondered.

And when the first record came out, I don't remember what music store it was. They had big sign-outs, you know, original Dixieland JASS band. Yeah. And my father was down there bright and early because Larry had wrote him and told him about it. And he got their first record.
Did you all have a phonograph at home with them?
Yeah, we, well, my dad went out and bought an old Victor Cranky or something.
And you, when you were a young kid, and when Larry was still around home, did you all have any phonograph then? I wondered what kind of records you heard, if you heard any at all.
I don't remember of us having a phonograph then. Well then.

Where would you think Larry got his inspiration, his idea of style? You got any idea? I really... Who would have been before him to... You know how everybody has somebody that they like very much in a jazz musical way.

Yeah, I think everybody is inspired, John, but I really don't know who inspired Larry. Maybe it could have been Freddie Burns. Because he was always at the house with my older brothers playing, you know. And I had three sisters and them, the girls in the neighborhood, you know, and the boys in the neighborhood. They'd give a little party in the house and of course my brothers would get King Watsky and Buzz Harvey and the guys to come over and they'd play, you know, and have a lot of fun.

Oh, by the way, while I think of it, what about the piano? Before the Dixieland, I understand they didn't usually use a piano. Some of the old bands used just bass and guitar or something. You know, is that true in the bands that Larry played with too at first? Did they have a piano or wait until late years or what?
I don't remember of a piano. No, they may have because I understand that the bands that played back of Basin Street used the piano.
Did you ever hear much music in the district or play in the district when you were still running yourself?
Well, I played one job there, yes. I was a kid. I didn't play very long.
Was it in one of the dance halls? Well, it was a regular club, I'd say.
Of course, I wasn't supposed to be back there because, you know, I was not old enough. But I played a little bit. I played with a little three-piece office.
I played with a piano. And Larry...
Oh, yeah. And Ray Nesha and myself, clarinet, piano and drums. Well, we had a piano. Well, that was after the Dixieland band.
They left and all.
Had gone to Chicago, yeah.
Had Larry ever played up there or do you know if he ever... Where back then?
...in the district? Oh, yeah. He played in the old tuxedo.
In the tuxedo dance hall.
Yeah.
Was that in the district or was it on this side of...
No, it was in the district. ...of Rampart Street?
No, it was on Franklin Street, right? Right in back of Lula White's. Was it?
Second block back, yeah. Well, I heard he mentioned that name, the old tuxedo. And that he played there. He played there, yeah.
Do you remember which band? I guess you couldn't have been there yourself to have heard him, so you wouldn't know who was there.

Well, he may have played with Emil Christian then. I'm not sure. We haven't talked to Emil very much. He may have played with Nick LaRocca at that time. I don't know. But you see, he went to Chicago before, I think it was before Nick, because when he first went to Chicago, he went with Tom Brown. And if I'm not mistaken, it was in the year of 1913 or 14.
There was a band, the Stein, the drummer, I think, the Stein took a band up too, about the time, a little bit before Nick went up too, I think.
Yeah, well...
I'm not sure how the dates are on that.

Well, I heard something about that. I don't know that to be a fact. But Nick did work with Stein, and I think it was when Larry joined the band. Stein and Larry took Yellow's place in the band. And I understand it was really Stein's band at first, then he left the band. I don't know why. I never heard. Larry never mentioned that. But I think it was... Nick told me that Stein left, and that was how they got Tony Spavaro. And that was when they called the band the original Dixieland.
Yeah, that's what I understood too.

Harry, your style is different from almost any other jazz clarinet player in the world. Completely different from your brother's style. And completely different from any other style I've ever had. It's a very lyrical and very melodic and a very creative style in the category of Bix Beiderback. I'm not saying that you copied from Bix Beiderback, but you know what I mean? Bix had a very lyrical style and each one of his notes counted. Can you put your finger on anybody who inspired you in your style? Or was it just an outgrowth of listening to all the good clarinet players and taking the best parts of each clarinet player? The best features of their style? Can you analyze your own style? Where it came from?
I really can't, John. I just... I don't know. I guess it's just a style that came to me. As I said before, Larry was very creative. And maybe it's sort of ran the family, by the way I see.
Well, your style isn't anything like Larry's. No, but... And yet it's a most beautiful style, I think. Well, I thought Larry's was too, but his ideas weren't similar to mine. No.
They were different. No. All together different. But very creative. Oh, very. Yeah.

And so I guess I just... Well, how was his tone? Of course, I've never heard him in person and all I can say is I heard up the records and you can't tell for sure. I mean, did he have a pretty big, full, loud tone? He must have at that album system. Yes.
To me, it's one of the jazziest tones I ever heard in jazz. To me.

You see, those very early recordings, you know, the recording wasn't so good in the beginning. You can't... It isn't fair to judge somebody by the... That's right, yeah. By the tone on those early recordings. I just wondered. Sounds good, you know, but I just wondered...

Yeah, I think it's marvelous, though, I'll tell you. He says tone is much better than you. I think your tone coming through on those early recordings is just wonderful to listen to. It's so clear. Yeah. Yeah, he is clear. He certainly comes out... It has so blooming much jazz sound in it. To me.

I had a letter at home that Larry got when he was in New York. He was with the Dixieland Band. He got a letter from someone, I think, in Minnesota. That was in the early years of radio. And they did a broadcast of radio. This fellow picks up the program and he listened. He was very attentive. Evidently a clarinet player. And he wrote Larry a letter about his tone. And he expressed himself in saying that... Larry's breathing... He said the way he would breathe, you know. He evidently even heard that. Well, myself, I wouldn't pay much attention to that. He said... And his clarinet must have been superb. You know, his... Well, everything was superb. There wasn't a click or nothing. His tone was so wonderful. And he asked Larry to write him. And he explained his tone. How he got the tone. How he would blow. What type of mouthpiece. And the reed he used. What kind of a clarinet. And all that, you know. I had the letter up until a couple of years ago. If it's still at home, I don't know. But I thought it was wonderful.
Yeah. Nice to have him. Appreciate it. That was in the early years of radio.
The early 20s. 1920s. The early 20s, yeah. And Larry kept that letter for years. I was just thinking about...

I was just thinking about... In the livery stable blues at the rooster call or whatever. Reminds me of Raymond Burke always said he doesn't like livery stable. He can't do that. He can't make livery stables. Do you know... Do you remember when you were a kid or anything when Larry first developed those things? Did he practice it at home or... Well, I don't remember... Do it on the job or under or anything?

I don't remember him practicing livery stable blues. Any tune in particular. But I remember when I was a kid, the clarinet players used to imitate birds, you know. Yeah. Different animals on the clarinet. You know. And I thought that... Well, I never did that myself.
Like you did on violin, you remember? Yeah.
Vaudible. Of course it was good. I thought it was real fine. I liked it, but I never did it myself. That's good.

Mm-hmm. Are there any other questions, Johnny? Or any suggestions? We still have a couple minutes on this reel. If there's... Anything about any of the old jobs that you can think of or any of the musicians you'd like to ask about?

Well, you know, I hadn't been playing professionally long when I joined Brownlee's band. And when I sat next to Harry, it was the first time that I'd ever played with anybody who really knew what he was doing in a professional way. Harry was a seasoned professional by the time I joined Brownlee's band. And I noticed that Harry played note-for-note harmony for everything that I played on cornet. Now, of course, when you fake, you can never play the same thing twice. It's impossible, unless you memorize a chorus or something like that. And very few people do that. Every time they play, just for the fun of it themselves, they play something a little different. Well, I noticed when I was with Brownlee that Harry played note-for-note harmony to whatever I did, regardless of how often I would change the way of playing, the pattern of the melody, which I played in this chorus. And I just took it for granted, you know, that all clarinet players did that. I didn't realize what I was sitting next to, you know, that this is still the only man alive that I have ever played with all over the country in the various bands that I've played in. And the only man alive that can do a thing like that, that I know of. Now, there may be others, but I remember not long ago at the St. Charles Hotel thinking of that. And I just try them out, you know, play, play different, as different as I could. And boy, that was a harmony. Son of a God has got an insight into what you're going to play next, or he can get there in such a hurry, you know, that nobody can detect that there's any lateness at all in getting there with a harmony, the proper harmony. That's a marvelous thing to have an ear like that. It's the most uncanny thing I've ever seen in my life in a jazz musician. It really is.

I know, it seems like a couple years ago, you told me, it seems like they were arranging, you mentioned how Harry can arrange pieces and can take his instrument and play the different notes to show the other colors.

Give it to the rest of the band, yeah. You take this note and you take this note. We'll work out a little introduction and Harry will say, here, you take this note and you take this note and so on. And that'll be the proper harmony for the introduction or the interlude or modulation or ending or whatever you want to call it.
Oh, just about out of this reel. If you have a few more minutes, do you have a few more minutes of your in your leg? You've been going in an hour now, don't I keep you? . . . . .
I was playing the piano, you know, my brother, he and I would play together and he would call out the notes, the piano notes.
Like A, B or B flat?

E flat, B flat, F and for quite a while I would say, which really was my G, I'd call it F, which was my F, I'd call it E flat because I thought Ed was right. So when I first started playing with Emmet Hardy, he knew the difference. So he'd say F, no, E flat for you, but it's really F, but you know it as E flat. So we'd play the tune, I'd play the harmony to him, you know, whatever he'd play.
I was going to ask, in regard to this arranging, head arranging or whatever you want to call it, when you think those things in your head, did you ever study any harmony or any theory?
I think that came natural, Bill.
Or ever play any piano to feel out those harmonies and chords? No, no, never did.
And yet you could hear it in your head all together somehow.
Did you start on chords?
Well, I play I can hear it, where as I go along I hear the harmony. Because I've always understood and felt as though the clarinet was really a harmony instrument.

Well how did you learn the chords? How did you know that the key of the chord of C has C, E, G in it and C minor, C, E flat, G. Did somebody tell you that in the beginning? Well... Was it just discussions in the band?
No, I just hear it, John. You'd hear people talk about it, huh? Probably. In the band, huh? Probably did, yeah, maybe.
But you never picked them out on... Nobody ever told you all the chords, huh?
No.
Tried to teach you all the various chords. You never tried to pick it out on the piano then?
No, I never did. To pick out the chords and things? I just figured it out, you know. You just grew up with it, huh?
Even the sixth, the diminished, and the ninth, and all that, the augments and all. I just figured out the chords myself.
On your own instrument?
I'd hear it, you know, I'd know just what...
Some people do have a marvelous gift for harmony, I've noticed that it's almost a bond with them.
Well, I... that's all I ever heard from kid on up, you know, music, music, and my...
Yeah, I guess there was discussion around the house all the time, and it just grew on you, huh?

It just grew on me, yeah. And Jim, he would, he always worked days, you know, he'd come home in the evening, he'd go right inside and pick up the fiddle and sit at the piano, you know, and my other brothers, they'd play, and of course I'd play the clarinet. I probably heard it, you know, and...
What kind of work did your brother Jim do? He was a painter. Painter?
Yeah, house painter.
Did you ever have a day job? Most musicians do have to fill in something in the daytime.
Oh yeah, I've worked house painting. Yeah. My father was a contractor.
Yeah.
Did Larry do any outside work when he was a kid? Larry was a house painter, yeah. He was too. Of course, Larry was a salesman too. Mm-hmm. He sold church goods, and...
Yeah.
I worked for a railroad for quite a few years. Electrician. Yeah.

Well, I was gonna ask while I think of it, if you have time to talk a minute about the, uh, brass bands. Did you ever play any street parades much? You mentioned you maybe played with Papa Lane once, but...
Oh, I played... Yeah, I played quite a few at, uh, Lane and different bands, you know.
Yeah. What were those, uh, for Mardi Gras or, uh, Carnival Time?
When were they? Yeah, yeah, I played, uh, Mardi Gras parades.

Um, Papa Lane talks about even, they used to play for funerals in the old days, like the David Crockett fire. Yeah, I understand that. Something like when they'd have some, death, they'd have a band after that. You don't remember any?
I've never played a funeral, and, uh, I don't remember. Yeah.
Uh, how big would these bands be that you played in on the street?
Oh, I'd say, well, sometimes two trumpets, uh, two cornets rather, and two trombones, tuba, and they'd have a baritone, upright out, clarinet, two drums. Yeah.
About ten or eleven pieces then. Yeah.
Uh-huh.
Uh, what, uh, kind of music did they play? Mostly marches, or they jazzed up things, or ragtime as they might have called it in those days, or what?
Well, I'd say it was ragtime.
Really ragtime. Yeah. No, no written arrangements then?
No, no. I've never played with a band that would read music.
Yeah. What kind of pieces did they play then? Do you remember any of the numbers on the street?
Yeah, just the regular popular tunes of the day, you know.
Wouldn't be things like Sousa Marches, or Stars and Stripes, or things like that ever, or anything of that kind?
I don't remember playing that, but I remember playing Pretty Baby, or anything?
Yeah.
Tunes like that.
And everybody would be faking their part and jazzing it up. Yeah.
Tiger rag. Blowing away, playing Tiger rag, yeah. Yeah.
Mm-hmm.
High Society. High Society, yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Mm-hmm. Yeah.
Those were standards then and still standards now. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Let's see, speaking of Tiger Rag, I think Jack Lane once, or maybe it was your friend, trombone player, or lives up in Jefferson, what's the matter? I can't think of it.
Oh, Happy Shilling.

Happy Shilling. Happy Shilling. Told about a clarinetist used to play with them, Eshiel Baque. Eshiel. And he might have been part colored or something, but anyway, he was very light. I've heard lots about him.
I wonder if you ever heard of that. In fact, I think I heard him play one time. I was told it was Eshiel, played very fine clarinet.
I never got to hear him. I think he-

I was a kid then, if I remember well, I was told it was Eshiel playing the clarinet. As I say, I used to go all over town, you know, wherever I hear, might be a band playing a dance, you know. I'd go down, stand outside and listen all night until the dance broke up.
I think you were a band. You folks didn't mind you learning music then, I guess, as long as Larry was in it too.
Well, my dad really didn't want us to learn. He wanted us to work, paint, you know. He'd paint us because he figured if we were out, which I'd stay out pretty late some nights playing.
Yeah.

Then wouldn't want to get up in the morning to go to work and Larry too. Because after Larry came back from the first trip, he went to Chicago, they flopped, and they went to New York and flopped. They had Ray Lopez on cornet then. We interviewed him in California. Tom Brown's man from Dixieland and Anilay Cano was on bass and piano. And Billy Lambeth on drums.
I never knew him. He was on bass and piano.

Yeah. And I understand they flopped. And when Larry came back home, my dad said, well, that's the end of it. Just, well, throw that thing away and come to work and forget the music. So Larry said, well, all right. And he went to work with my dad. One afternoon, Tom Brown came to the house. And he said, well, I'm going to go to work with him. So Larry told my dad, he looked out, he said, it's Tom Brown out there. So my dad said, I'll go talk to him. So he went out and he said, Tommy said, now look, Brown, if you're coming here to get this boy to go away again, you just won't forget about it. Now he's back working and I don't want him to go up there and starve. So Tom said, oh no, Mr. Shields, this is the real McCoy this time. He said, here it is, here. You read this telegram and we're going to make so much. And this is it now. Larry was talking to my mother at the time in the kitchen. Of course, you know, the mother liked, she said. Our dad come in, Tom came in with him. Tom was very insistent. I'm glad he was at the time. So Tom started talking to my mother. My mother said, well, if the boy wants to go, he's not happy painting. He wants to play music. Let him go. So she said, you sure you want to go? Larry said, yes, I want to go. All right. My dad said, well, okay. Your mother says, let you go. Go ahead. So he did, but something happened in Chicago. He left Brown's band. And I think he swapped jobs with Gussie Miller.
What's that? Gussie Miller was very good.

Gussie can tell you that. I heard that. Somebody told me that. And he went to work at White City and Gussie Miller went to work with Tom Brown at the College Inn, I think it was, in Chicago. And then Larry didn't like working with this big band out in White City. And just about that time, Yellow quit Nick LaRocca. And so they asked Larry to join the band. So Larry said, well, Yellow quit. All right. He said, I don't like this outfit I'm with now. No. So Larry joined Nick then. And then he left the casino garden and said, what in New York? You got to make it money.
Did he seem to like the traveling around or get homesick do you think?

Well, Larry never mentioned being homesick. He used to write my mother at least one letter every week. And of course he'd write us time to time. Write my dad. He was doing all right. Making money. They were going over big. And so, and when they, he wrote and said they were going to London. So my mother, don't worry about me. But of course he was married by that time.
Was married.
Yeah. And his wife was New York with him. She married a Chicago girl. She's still living in California. Yeah. And, but my mother did worry, you know. Sure.
Of course.
But they did real well over in New York. And they came back and he stayed with the band. I think until 1924 or 25.

Yeah. They made some even late records there. Okay. And some, some of the victors are pretty late. Uh huh. After he came back here, did he work much at music or started to give it up from there? Larry.
No, he gave it up. Yeah.
Until they had that come back in 1936 or so. Yeah.

Uh huh. Then after that, he didn't play anymore. Yeah. Didn't play at all after that. No. He just retired, but, uh, he lived out in, uh, Hollywood. But every night, uh, I understand he'd go over and see Joe Rushkin, who was a very good friend of his. Joe was working at the Brown Derby, I think was Red Nickels. Yeah. And he'd always go around and see the guys, you know, and listen. And, uh, as I understand, he, he and Joe Frisco would sit around and talk to him. And so he, I think, uh, their first job, which was, uh, Tom Brown's band was with Joe Frisco.
I remember, um,
He took them to Chicago. Yeah.

First time. And he was, uh, Tom Brown showed us a letter. He had written to Joe, uh, Tom and he had written to Frisco. You know, that's when Nick was trying to say he was the first one to go to Chicago or something. And I think they had a letter from Joe Frisco saying that he hired Tom Brown. Uh huh. On a certain date, you know, they were. That's right.

Trying to show that they. I understand, uh, he was working up here at Farmer, cause it's Ratskiller. That was a restaurant up here. Who, who was that? Tom Brown? No, Joe Frisco was dancing up there then. Uh huh. And he heard the band. They were advertising a prize fight or something. Brown's band. And he liked the band. And he told him that he could place them on a job in Chicago. But they flopped. Whether he worked with the band or not, I don't know. He may have had. He may have booked, uh, the band with him, but they flopped in Chicago.
Yeah.
And they went on to New York as an act. They worked in Broadville. They flopped in New York. Uh, Arnold Loi Canna can tell you all about that. Yeah. He was with the bunch. Yeah.
And we talked to Ray, uh, Lopez. Ray Lopez. I was clear he told us some of that history and, uh, saw him two years ago in California.
Uh huh.
Do you remember hearing Ray Lopez around here much?
I heard him at my house when I was a kid. Oh, yeah. Yeah. They, he, he also played with my brother Jimmy. Oh, you did?
And King Walski.
He might have mentioned him.
He played the cornets, yeah.
Yeah, you might have mentioned him even when I interviewed him.
I can't remember what they all tell him.
Uh huh. Well, Ray was, uh, pretty young then I'd imagine. He and Larry both. And I think that was about the first time he and Larry got together. Yeah. Played together.
What style did he play? A style like Johnny Lalo?
I really don't remember John, no. I imagine he did play that style because that was, uh, about the style most trumpet players played. Yeah. I mean, cornet plays.
What do you think about the saxophone that puts you on the spot? I mean, you say you've played sax a little. Do you like it as well as clarinet? No, no, I don't.
I like the clarinet. I like to listen to saxophone. Personally, I like the clarinet. I've heard some very fine saxophone players, but I don't like to play it too much.
But should you play alto or tenor?
I play tenor mostly. Tenor. I like the clarinet. Well, you can tell that from the way you play. You must stay with it a few years. I like to listen to saxophone, but I don't like to play it.
I've heard some very fine saxophone players, like Eddie Miller.
To me, he's the great one. He plays awful fine. That's great. I've heard some very fine saxophone players, like Eddie Miller. Yeah. To me, he's the great one. He plays awful fine.
He plays beautifully. I like it.
I'm telling you, right? I go out of my way just to listen to him. Yeah. That's the Bouchon, isn't it? Yeah, he plays. He certainly is.
Great.
Yeah. Great.
Did they use the sax in the old days when your brother and you were coming up? No. When did they come in?

I think there was only one saxophone player around New Orleans then, and he played a double octave saxophone around New Orleans here. He was from Mexico. His name was Mr. Ramos. Oh. And he was about the only saxophone player. You mean double octave?
Is that low? A big?

Well, it was the first saxophone, the first one's bill. They had to use the double octave before they devised this way of having the octave work both ways from high to low register. At that time, the saxophone he used, he'd have to switch from one octave to the other to play from low to high, from high to low.

Let's make, like they call it like a double bassoon is a great big long, twice as long or something. Uh huh. It wasn't a real low like baritone or anything. What? The sax, the first sax. Oh, that same, alto and the tenor.
The alto along in the... Mr. Ramos played the tenor when I heard him.
I guess the... See, melodies were great in those days.

Well, that was later on when they began using the saxophone. Most of the saxophone players used to see melody. My voice saxophone was the C melody. And I bought an alto. You had C melody? I played it for a while. I think I played it for a while with Brownlee.
Yeah. You played sax some, but you played clarinet mostly. Mostly clarinet.

Yeah. I played the baritone too then with Brownlee. But then when I joined Sharky, or rather rejoined Sharky, I played the tenor. Oh. Because he used Sidney Aragon, who played nothing but the clarinet.
Can you tell us anything about him? I never got to meet him. Sidney? Raymond talks a lot about him, but...
Sidney? I thought Sidney was one of the finest clarinet players I ever listened to. Sounds fine on records.
Oh, wonderful.
Sidney was.
Yeah.
Yeah, he played wonderful.
You and Sidney used to work beautifully at the ringside. You remember? We worked very good. In that little band?
Two clarinets and a cornet. Sharky on the cornet. Two clarinets. Two clarinets. He had a wonderful ear. It's a marvelous instrumentation. You'd be surprised.

I've often wanted to get these two guys together, Ram and Burke and Harry. Well, Joe Barrett did get you together a couple of times, but then you did it for three. Yeah, but it wasn't done in that way. It wasn't done in the right way. This has got to be rehearsed, what Harry does.
How big a rhythm section?
Well, just a three-piece rhythm section, that's all.

Just no trombone. When Sid and I played together, he had a marvelous ear, Sidney. He didn't read music, but he had a wonderful ear. And he would, if he phrased one way, well, I'd go with him. Or if I phrased a certain way, he'd go with me. See, he had a very sharp ear. And we'd always work with the cornet, both of us. If he played a fifth, I'd play the third, to the lead. Yeah. And we got along fine. And a lot of the stuff, we had little things worked up together, you know, little, what might I say, arrangements. Head arrangements. Head arrangements. Head arrangements. Head arrangements. And we'd work them up together. And we'd, our harmony might not have been perfect, but it sounded good.
It was one of the cutest bands. One of the cutest bands I ever heard. It really was. That was at the ringside.
Yeah. The ringside.
Where was that, by the way? It's not around now.
It's the same place now.
It's never changed. It's still up.

Oh, what do they call it now? They call it something. Pete Herman's. Oh, Pete Herman's place. Pete Herman's place, yeah. Pete Herman's place, yeah. Uh-huh. It was called the ringside in those days, yeah.
It seems like somebody said it was called the orchard or something. At one time it was the orchard.
I remember when it was the orchard.
Somebody said they had grapes or something all around the front, like bushes or something, or vines. I don't know if they painted it on. Yeah, right. Or do they have them? Leaves and, you know.
Yeah. That's a sound that has got to be gotten again in jazz. I tell you, it's too good to, not to do more of. And I won't forget listening to that little group down there. Yeah.
Of course, they were all good men. And, uh, they... Who was the rhythm section, remember? Who else was... How was that? Who was the rhythm section, the piano and...
Oh, uh, Joe Caprero played banjo.
Banjo.
And, uh, Martin Abraham, chink. Yeah, chink. Played bass. And Freddie Newman on piano. Yeah. Augie Chalang played drums. Very fine.
Yeah, it'd be a nice band all together. Real fine.
Mm-hmm. I thought it was one of the best bands that was ever organized in the city of New Orleans.
It certainly was a very fine organization. It really was at that time. It really was at that time. It was.
I thought at that time we were way ahead of our time.
I heard, I heard sounds from that band.
You know, the harmony and the tunes we played at that time were... Yeah.

Those two clarinets, the way they worked together, gave a sound which I've never heard. Yeah. Before or since. That's the reason I've been so eager to try to get that worked out with Harry and Raymond.
I thought Sidney and I worked together very, very good. Very close. Yeah, I bet.
Yeah, Raymond.
Raymond's a very fine clarinet player. He has very sharp ear.
Yeah. Gets a beautiful tone and all too.
Oh, beautiful. Beautiful tone.
Especially down low register.
Yeah.
Doesn't play much up high usually like you do. Oh, he plays very high up high. You cover the high instrument. Yeah, he can too. Yeah, he can too. Yeah.
To my estimation, Raymond's one of the best.

Well, I was wondering, to get back to that low register business, one of those English records, the original Dixieland made over there, had a solo by your brother all in the low register, which he didn't usually do in the other records. Yeah, I had that record. Did he ever play that way much around here? That is, did he keep going up and down covering the whole instrument or did he sometimes just stick to one register for a solo?

Well, I really don't remember, but Larry got a beautiful tone in the low register. Yeah. Now at that time, the equipment for recording, of course, you know what it was then. So his low register, I thought even though he played in the horn and the recording, you know, wasn't just, but his tone was really beautiful, I thought. Yeah. I'm forever blowing bubbles, you, you thinking of, huh?

I don't remember that, that's the title, it seems like another title to me too. I'm forever blowing bubbles. I don't have the record here now, it seems like some other tune that Joe Merez used later then too. A pop tune that he played that on.
Well, that was the only English recording that I heard. Did you use that low? That he played in the low register.
I think, this one just came out, but it must have been out in the old days too. Yeah. You have those old ones on Columbia, the 78s, or is that a long play that you have?
The Columbia? That's the English. Yeah, the English. Yeah, I had those, the 78s. Yeah, on 78, I never did get them on 78s.
I've still got a couple of them.
Still got some of them.

Those are hard to find in this country though. Oh yeah. Rare records. Were there any other records you made you started, we might talk a minute about that. You mentioned the Brown Lee records. Anything else in the old days then, until you began recording with Johnny?
No, that was the only recording I made. That old kid.
Any other numbers that you composed that you can...
Well... I wrote a tune when I was with the Dukes of Tiximans, if that's what you're referring to.
Yeah, anything like that is alright.
Yeah, well, they, the manager of the band suggested that we would name it 339 March. So we recorded it on the Columbia record. Yeah. Called it 339 March. That's all the printout too.
I thought it was a pretty good tune.
It sounds pretty good to me. It's a pretty good recording. Though I don't have it. I don't have too many of my own recordings. Didn't bother to save them. No, I have the ones I made with Johnny.
Yeah.
And a few I made with Joe Moritz.

Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Well that one you made with Johnny with the St. Louis blues and all on is beautiful. Yeah, I got that. In particular, that St. Louis blues, in addition to your brother's chorus, some of those other low notes and chords.

Well, I still use that chorus whenever I play St. Louis blues. I wouldn't play another chorus, to tell you the truth. Because I love that chorus. Yeah. And I, I'll always play it. It's a beautiful chorus.
And they published that in the arrangement of it too, that Melrose edition has that chorus written out.
I think that was one of the finest clarinet chorus that we ever played or ever recorded. So I'll continue to play that.
That's real creating.
Yes, I think so.

Anything else, else about some of the later jobs you've played? I know you worked with Sharkey for years and of course you worked with Johnny on that job when you recorded. You just got back from Nix, I understand. From Nix, yeah, New York.
We were, we were there, I'd say, well, I worked there about two and a half, three months.
Mm-hmm.
And the band just finished there. They, I think they worked another month after I left the band. Whose band was it?
Roy Liberto.
Roy Liberto.
Do they play free jazz like we do?
I had to come to my county sickness at home. Yeah.

Did they play, did, did, did Liberto play free jazz like we play around here, you know? Well. Or was it sort of arranged? With introductions and things like that. Well, it was sort of arranged. It had introductions worked out and things like that.
Yeah, it was more modern, I think, John. Yeah. All the fellows from New Orleans here?
No. Or did you pick up some there? No.

We, uh, he has a boy from St. Louis plays very, very fine trombone. Young fellow, only 24 years old. Young fellow by the name of Jimmy Haislip, marvelous trombone player. Yeah. I predict that he'll be one of the finest. In fact, I'll say he might be the finest in the country in a few more years if he continues to, to go along this year.
How's the Dixieland style going in New York? Is it still popular? Oh, yeah, yeah. Did you hear much other music around?
Yeah, yeah, they, people seem to like it.
Is Nick's packed every night?

Well, I wouldn't say every night, John, but they sure do their share of business. Yeah. And, of course, weekends there, why, the place is just jammed, you know. And, uh, every night they have their quota, you know, people. And also the Metropole, they... They're just about here. Of course, they, they use both the... Modern and... And Dick's 20. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
They're all my favorite. I like them all and every tune I play I like what I play.
What about the blues in general? Do you like to make up the blues that way?
I love the blues because you can create as you go along. And of course as you play the blues you're inspired.
I like the blues very much.
I do like the blues.
Is there anything about the tempo that is to me it seems sometimes they play everything faster. Well to mention one record that you made too I guess you remember the Tiger Rag Stampede. Oh yeah.
Well believe me I was playing with Leverda in New York. Now he plays just about twice that fast. Really? As we recorded it.
Yeah. But in the old age.
Yeah he plays it much faster because I don't know the people seem to like it. Yeah it seems. The public in general.
Maybe they think that's hot stuff when it goes fast. I imagine so. In the old days did they ever play anything fast like that fast?
Not that fast.
You can't play anything pretty in that fast tempo can you? No. No. They never played that fast. Just a wild sound.
Well might I say that it's more showmanship than the old days. Yeah I get it. You've got to be a pretty good showman now. And that counts a lot.
Well anyway I guess it pays a little bit more money than it did. Oh it does. Sometimes in the old days.
Right. Sure.
When you all were working for those some of those joints that they paid very little did you get pretty good tips in the old days though or? No.
No. No. No we didn't. Well during the depression.
Of course during the depression everybody was on the rocks.
We worked for peanuts. Yeah. But most of us worked though because we liked it. Of course that was guys who were single like myself. I loved it. I didn't make a lot of money but I had a lot of fun.
The colored guys tell about they had a big WPA band during the depression. Did they have a white band like that too? Yes. I didn't know much about that.
Yes I understand they did. In fact I knew a couple of the guys that worked with the white WPA band.
I never heard much about it. Anyway I hope those days are gone forever.
I hope so.
Well I think that just about winds it up here.
Well.

segments.title: Opening: Wiggs asks about Emmett Hardy's style
segments.summary: Bill Russell dates the interview, and Johnny Wiggs asks Harry about Emmett Hardy's style, since Harry played with him in Brownlee's band more than anyone.

segments.title: Emmett Hardy's first band at Midway Park
segments.summary: Harry recalls Emmett's first band opening Midway Park across the river, and says Emmett played fine cornet in an original style.

segments.title: Birth date, father the dancer, musical mother's family, half brothers
segments.summary: Harry gives his birth year (1899) and name, says his father danced, his mother's brothers and mother played strings, and he had half brothers John and James Ruth.

segments.title: Kid band with brother Ed, Emmett and Charlie Leach
segments.summary: Harry's brother Ed played piano in a little band with Emmett, Charlie Leach, Donald Coleman and others, rehearsing at Leach's house.

segments.title: Kansas City convention trip with the boys' band
segments.summary: The kids' band went to a Grotto convention in Kansas City, got newspaper coverage, then played small local jobs; Ed died in 1938.

segments.title: Learning clarinet from Larry
segments.summary: Larry started Harry on clarinet at about eight, later sent his old thirteen-key Buffet from Chicago, and brother Jimmy helped; Harry taught himself to read a little.

segments.title: First band with Pansy Lane and early jobs
segments.summary: Harry's first job was with Alfred 'Pansy' Lane, then the Pup Cafe and Raleigh Rye with Ed, before he quit to work for his father.

segments.title: Childhood home and neighbor Buddy Bolin
segments.summary: He was born at 2319 First Street, moved to Third and Clara around age five or six, and later to Broadmoor. Harry relays what his brothers and half sister told him about Buddy Bolin, a fine cornetist who was confined as mentally ill and later played trombone; Russell gives his dates.

segments.title: Listening to Johnny Dodds at Naulties Hall
segments.summary: As a boy Harry sat outside Naulties Hall to hear Johnny Dodds and Joe Oliver, and liked other clarinetists, around World War I.

segments.title: Colored bands at National Baseball Park
segments.summary: Harry listened from the Claiborne Canal bank to Sam Morgan, Kid Rena and Punch Miller at Monday dances on platforms at the ballpark, sometimes with Emmett.

segments.chapter: Larry Shields and the Dixieland Band
segments.title: Papa Jack Laine's band and the Brunies brothers
segments.summary: Harry says Larry played with Jack Laine's bands; Russell reports on Laine; Harry played one parade job with Laine's son.

segments.chapter: Larry Shields and the Dixieland Band
segments.title: Larry's marching bands and Clem Camp
segments.summary: Harry says Laine gave many players their start, and tells of Larry in marching bands and the St. Francis de Sales Band with clarinetist Clem Camp.

segments.chapter: Larry Shields and the Dixieland Band
segments.title: Yellow Nunez, the C clarinet and Brownlee
segments.summary: Harry and Wiggs discuss Yellow Nunez, a fine clarinetist who played a C Albert-system clarinet, and his few jobs with Brownlee.

segments.chapter: Larry Shields and the Dixieland Band
segments.title: Harry's saxophone and Larry's later big-band work
segments.summary: Harry says he played saxophone but never E flat clarinet; Larry played sax and clarinet in California big bands and shows.

segments.chapter: Larry Shields and the Dixieland Band
segments.title: How Larry got his first clarinet from Freddie Burns
segments.summary: Larry began at 15 or 16, buying his first clarinet from Freddie Burns, who played with Jimmy and King Watsky; Larry was self-taught.

segments.chapter: Larry Shields and the Dixieland Band
segments.title: Mother's family string band and early jazz
segments.summary: Harry's mother, who died at 94 in 1948, said her brothers' string band with a flute played by ear, mazurkas and ragtime, which Harry takes as early jazz.

segments.chapter: Larry Shields and the Dixieland Band
segments.title: Origin of the word 'jazz' and the Dixieland Band
segments.summary: Harry relays Larry's story of the name jazz at the Casino Gardens in Chicago and the changing J-A-S spelling, and says earlier bands played a less modern style.

segments.title: Larry's Fournier reeds and Buffet clarinet
segments.summary: Larry searched for good reeds and found French Fournier reeds, buying a supply and using a Buffet seventeen-key clarinet.

segments.title: Why Harry prefers the Albert system
segments.summary: Harry and the others compare Albert and Boehm clarinets and tone, naming players such as Kenny Devine, Benny Goodman and Tony Parenti.

segments.title: Reed strength and the Alberts Kenny Devine gave him
segments.summary: Harry uses a two or two-and-a-half reed, explains the full Albert system, and says Kenny Devine gave him two Alberts in New York.

segments.title: Larry's advice: relax and avoid pressure
segments.summary: Asked for tone secrets, Harry says Larry only told him to relax and not bite, and that Larry used medium reeds.

segments.title: Playing with Brownlee, Sharky Bonanno and Tom Brown
segments.summary: Harry lists early work with Norman Brownlee, Johnny Wiggs and Sharky Bonanno, and playing with Tom Brown.

segments.title: The 1924-25 Brownlee records and 'Peculiar Rag'
segments.summary: Harry dates his first records to 1924-25 with Brownlee, tells of sharing composer credit on 'Peculiar' and 'Dirty Rag', and Russell reports on Brownlee in Pensacola.

segments.title: Brownlee's engagements, seven nights a week
segments.summary: Harry describes the round of dances, lodges and school jobs, with Midway the steady one, and Brownlee handing out each week's jobs.

segments.title: The Midway Park pavilion and Everett Thomas
segments.summary: Harry, Wiggs and Russell reconstruct Midway Park: an open-air dance pavilion near the Harvey Canal, how it opened and who ran it.

segments.chapter: Larry in Chicago and New York
segments.title: Offers to join Durante in New York; Dixieland Band piano changes
segments.summary: Harry's mother kept him home when Jimmy Durante and Frank Christian wanted him; he relates the ODJB's pianist changes up to Billy Jones in London.

segments.chapter: Larry in Chicago and New York
segments.title: Larry's letters and New Orleans reaction to the records
segments.summary: Larry wrote home weekly, the first record drew local pride, Harry's father bought it and a Victrola, and the family had no phonograph earlier.

segments.chapter: Larry in Chicago and New York
segments.title: Where Larry's style came from
segments.summary: Wiggs asks who inspired Larry; Harry guesses Freddie Burns and describes house parties with his brothers' friends.

segments.chapter: Larry in Chicago and New York
segments.title: Pianos in bands and one job in the District
segments.summary: Harry says early bands often had no piano, and tells of one job as a boy in a back-of-town club in a trio.

segments.chapter: Larry in Chicago and New York
segments.title: Larry at the Tuxedo, going to Chicago with Tom Brown, and Stein's band
segments.summary: Larry played in the Tuxedo dance hall and went to Chicago with Tom Brown about 1913-14; Harry relays how Stein's band became the Original Dixieland Band.

segments.title: Wiggs asks Harry about his own lyrical style
segments.summary: Wiggs praises Harry's lyrical, creative style and compares it to Bix; Harry cannot say where it came from and says it differs from Larry's.

segments.title: A fan letter about Larry's tone; bird imitations
