segments.summary: Harry recalls a radio listener's letter praising Larry's tone, and clarinetists imitating animals, but says he never did that.

segments.title: Wiggs on Harry's note-for-note harmony
segments.summary: Wiggs says that when he played next to Harry in Brownlee's band, Harry harmonised every note he played, and that Harry can arrange parts by ear.

segments.title: Ed calling notes: learning keys on clarinet
segments.summary: Harry's brother Ed called out piano notes, so Harry thought in transposed names, which Emmett Hardy later corrected.

segments.title: Hearing harmony by ear without theory
segments.summary: Harry says he never studied harmony or piano, figured out chords himself, and grew up with music at home.

segments.title: Day jobs: house painting and railroad electrician
segments.summary: Harry, Jim and Larry painted houses; Larry sold church goods, and Harry worked for a railroad as an electrician.

segments.title: Street parade bands and their ragtime repertoire
segments.summary: Harry describes ten-piece street bands playing Mardi Gras parades without written music: popular tunes like Pretty Baby, Tiger Rag and High Society.

segments.title: Eshiel, a light-skinned clarinetist Harry heard as a kid
segments.summary: Russell asks about Eshiel Baque, who played with Laine's players; Harry thinks he heard him once and describes wandering town to hear bands.

segments.chapter: Larry in Chicago and New York
segments.title: Father's reluctance; Larry returns from the New York flop and leaves again with Tom Brown
segments.summary: Harry's father wanted the boys to paint; after the Brown band flopped in Chicago and New York, Larry returned, then left again after Tom Brown persuaded the parents, and Larry ended up with Nick LaRocca.

segments.chapter: Larry in Chicago and New York
segments.title: Larry's years with the Dixieland Band and retirement
segments.summary: Larry wrote home weekly, married a Chicago girl, stayed with the band to 1924-25, then quit music and later lived in Hollywood.

segments.chapter: Larry in Chicago and New York
segments.title: Joe Frisco and Tom Brown's band
segments.summary: Harry and Russell trace how Joe Frisco heard Brown's band in New Orleans, took them to Chicago, and the band flopped in Chicago and New York.

segments.chapter: Larry in Chicago and New York
segments.title: Ray Lopez
segments.summary: Harry heard Ray Lopez at his house as a kid, where he played with Jimmy, and thinks he first played with Larry then, in the style of cornetists of the time.

segments.title: Harry on saxophone and Eddie Miller
segments.summary: Harry prefers clarinet to saxophone, plays tenor, and greatly admires Eddie Miller.

segments.title: Early saxophone in New Orleans and Harry's sax with Brownlee
segments.summary: Harry says Mr. Ramos was nearly the only saxophonist in early days; Harry played C melody, alto and baritone with Brownlee.

segments.chapter: Sharky Bonanno, Sidney Arodin and the Ringside
segments.title: Two clarinets with Sharky Bonanno and Sidney Arodin at the Ringside
segments.summary: Harry rejoined Sharky and played with clarinetist Sidney Arodin; they worked out head arrangements, and Wiggs remembers the band.

segments.chapter: Sharky Bonanno, Sidney Arodin and the Ringside
segments.title: Where the Ringside was
segments.summary: They place the Ringside, later Pete Herman's, earlier the Orchard.

segments.chapter: Sharky Bonanno, Sidney Arodin and the Ringside
segments.title: The Ringside rhythm section and why the band was ahead of its time
segments.summary: Harry names the rhythm section and says it was one of the best New Orleans bands, with two clarinets making a unique sound. They then praise Raymond Burke's ear and tone.

segments.chapter: Recordings, later jobs and changing times
segments.title: Larry's low register on the English records
segments.summary: Russell asks about Larry's low-register solo on an English Columbia record; Harry admires his low tone and recalls hearing only that record.

segments.chapter: Recordings, later jobs and changing times
segments.title: Harry's own recordings: '339 March' and 'St. Louis Blues'
segments.summary: Harry says the Brownlee records were his only early recording, tells of '339 March', and the St. Louis Blues chorus with Wiggs, based on Larry's.

segments.chapter: Recordings, later jobs and changing times
segments.title: Working with Roy Liberto in New York
segments.summary: Harry just got back from a few months with Roy Liberto's band, which was more arranged, and describes Dixieland clubs in New York.

segments.chapter: Recordings, later jobs and changing times
segments.title: Liking the blues; modern fast tempos and showmanship
segments.summary: Harry loves creating in the blues; he finds current Tiger Rag tempos twice as fast as the old record and ascribes this to showmanship.

segments.chapter: Recordings, later jobs and changing times
segments.title: Pay, tips, the Depression and the WPA band
segments.summary: They discuss low pay and no tips in the Depression, working for fun, and a white WPA band.

segments.chapter: Recordings, later jobs and changing times
segments.title: Closing
segments.summary: Russell winds up the interview.
